transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Redwood Infra), Maya Torres (Orchid ML), Caleb Nguyen (Orchid Platform), Priyanka Rao (Orchid Security)

[00:00] Alex: okay, thanks everyone for joining. uh we'll try to keep this tight — main goal is to surface the regression you're seeing after the quantize step, and then map to a playbook for private deployments. thanks for sending the initial artifacts, Maya.
[00:18] Maya: yeah thanks — and thanks for the quick follow-up. we ran a GPTQ flow last week on our internal 7B-like model and saw a 3.6% drop on the QA bench, which is... ya, enough to block rollout.
[00:30] Samira: mm-hmm. can you say a little more about the bench? is it prompt distribution aligned with prod?
[00:38] Maya: mostly. it's a ~1k prompt set — a mix of short Q/A and multi-turn clinical triage type prompts. we kept few-shot context, and we also have a set without prefix to check prefix sensitivity.
[00:50] Alex: okay, good. initial hypothesis from artifacts you sent: two buckets — (a) quantization-induced logit shifts on a small subset of layers, (b) KV-cache / prefix interaction causing decode misalignment when combined with batching. we need to prove both.
[01:05] Caleb: right — we see the regression more often when we enable batch size > 1, which is odd because our prior unquantized runs were fine.
[01:12] Jon: that points to ordering and KV index alignment problems or numerical underflow when mixing cached KV with newly computed keys in quantized kernels.
[01:20] Samira: we also noticed that AWQ produced slightly better top-1 accuracy than straight GPTQ on your model in our quick tests, but AWQ throughput was lower until we tuned kernels.
[01:31] Maya: AWQ? we thought AWQ was a newer algorithm — can you give a quick diff between GPTQ and AWQ in practice?
[01:36] Samira: sure. short: GPTQ is a per-weight quantization with a post-hoc calibration using reconstruction loss; AWQ applies asymmetric weight quant and typically preserves outlier activations better but has different calibration heuristics. AWQ tends to need slightly different scale factors per layer and can handle activation distributions with heavier tails.
[01:54] Priyanka: for security, anything about quantization changes we should be worried about? like side channels or determinism differences in private vs hosted?
[02:03] Alex: good call — determinism is a concern. quantized kernels, especially with stochastic rounding or fused operators, can produce non-bit-identical outputs across hardware or runs. For auditability we log model and quantization profile checksums, and for Private deployments we can pin a deterministic compute path (disable stochastic rounding) as part of the deployment profile.
[02:21] Caleb: can that increase error? I mean disabling stochastic rounding might make some noise worse right?
[02:26] Samira: it can. stochastic rounding sometimes helps reduce systematic bias at the cost of reproducibility. our rollout playbook typically starts with non-stochastic (deterministic) for safety and if accuracy suffers we test stochastic rounding in a controlled A/B.
[02:39] Alex: okay let's talk layerwise regressions — from the diffs you sent, the biggest logit perturbations are in layers 23-26 and the last layer norm. that suggests either: calibration data mismatch during GPTQ, or sensitivity to scaling in attention heads at those layers.
[02:56] Maya: we used a small calibration set from dev, ~200 examples — that might be the issue.
[03:00] Samira: yeah 200 is risky for some models. we recommend 2k-5k diverse prompts for calibration, or per-layer calibration with more examples for attention-dense layers.
[03:10] Jon: also from an infra lens, when we do on-prem quantized runs we see reduced FP cache precision for KV if you use half-precision caches with int8 weights, which can cause mismatch when you mix cached keys from an unquantized warmup run.
[03:24] Caleb: interesting — so warmup policy matters. we had a strategy where cache was populated by a small warmup unquantized pass. maybe that's the bug.
[03:32] Samira: that would explain the batch sensitivity. if the first request yields cached keys in FP32 while subsequent per-token kernels use quantized weight paths with scaled ops, you can get slight phase shifts in softmax leading to different tokens.
[03:44] Maya: hmm. so do you recommend regenerating cache post-quantize? that's expensive.
[03:48] Alex: tradeoffs. options: (1) regenerate cache after model quantization for warmup requests, (2) keep cache format independent and cast at read-time — more CPU overhead but safe, (3) use runtime fallback to FP16 for first N tokens of a prefix to align computation.
[04:03] Priyanka: option 2 with cast at read-time — would that create data retention issues? we're paranoid about copies in memory.
[04:10] Jon: it's just runtime memory copy; in Private we can limit visibility and ensure memory is ephemeral. encryption-in-use is trickier but our runtime supports KMS-backed keys and encrypted memory mappings for HSM setups.
[04:20] Samira: back to accuracy — we should quantify the effect of batch size cross product with cache handling. recommended test matrix: batch sizes [1,4,8], cache policies [no-cache, prewarm-unquantized, prewarm-quantized], quant methods [GPTQ, AWQ, Hybrid INT8, FP8 simulated].
[04:38] Maya: can Redwood run that matrix for us or we run it in-house?
[04:42] Alex: we can run baseline runs in our dedicated test infra; for on-prem we'll provide the perf harness and scripts so you can reproduce. agreed?
[04:48] Caleb: yes please provide the harness. reproducibility is key for us.
[04:53] Samira: noted — we'll include exact seed control, RNG settings, and whether stochastic rounding is enabled.
[04:58] Alex: good. next area: batching and latency SLOs. quantization usually reduces arithmetic cost per op but may complicate batching due to kernel tiling differences. Samira, did you see kernel throughput drop on smaller sequences?
[05:12] Samira: for sequences < 64 tokens on INT8 fused kernels we saw slightly higher per-token latency vs FP16 on GPU X when batch size small — the overhead of quant-dequant and extra memory copies dominated. At batch >= 4 it wins hands down.
[05:25] Maya: that's our workload — many short interactions. latency matters more than throughput.
[05:29] Alex: that's critical. our recommendation: for short-text SLOs prefer hybrid approach — keep last n layers in FP16 or FP8 and quantize earlier layers. that keeps early attention compute cheaper but preserves final response quality; also it avoids costly dequant at tail.
[05:44] Caleb: hybrid per-layer quantization — does Redwood provide automated layer selection?
[05:48] Samira: yes, our optimize tool suggests a per-layer quant profile given a target SLO and accuracy loss threshold. it ranks layers by sensitivity and gives a suggestion like quantize layers 1-16 INT8, keep 17-32 FP16. but we still need to validate in your bench.
[06:00] Priyanka: security question again — are any quantized artifacts considered secrets? like the scale tables or calibration sets?
[06:06] Alex: the calibration set is sensitive if it contains PII. scale tables are model artifacts; we treat them as part of the model bundle. for Private we support encrypted model blobs and KMS unwrapping at load.
[06:15] Maya: okay, concrete asks from our side: (1) can you triage whether the 3.6% drop is mainly layerwise or cache+batch issue, (2) recommend a precise rollout path we can follow on Private, and (3) provide a kernel-level perf baseline for our onprem GPU (A100-v5).
[06:31] Alex: yes. triage plan: run layerwise ablation — quantize single layer groups and measure metrics; run caching matrix; run GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8 on the 1k prompt set. We'll produce a short report and recommended hybrid profile.
[06:43] Samira: we'll also capture per-token logit diffs and a small set of failing prompt traces to identify common failure modes (e.g., hallucination vs drop-in entity recall).
[06:52] Maya: sounds good. one more thing — we saw two specific failures where the model hallucinated a medication dosage after quantization. that's high severity for us.
[07:00] Priyanka: yeah that's our redline. even if overall accuracy drops 3%, specific clinical hallucinations are unacceptable.
[07:05] Jon: in those cases we want to know if it's a change in softmax peak or a different token sampled due to RNG. logging full token-level probabilities for audit will help.
[07:14] Alex: agreed. we'll include token-prob deltas in the report. also recommend adding an explicit guard in the prompt pipeline for medication terms with a safety re-ranker during pilot.
[07:25] Caleb: re-ranker might add latency; can we do an async check?
[07:28] Samira: yes, you can run a fast logit-check re-ranker in a separate thread and if risky content found, fall back to FP16 path synchronously. it's a classic safety/cost tradeoff.
[07:38] Maya: about rollout playbook — what are the typical stages you recommend for Private? a/b canary?
[07:43] Alex: recommended: (1) internal QA tests (dev set with 5k prompts), (2) small canary with 1% of traffic pinned to quantized model with synchronous logging, (3) expand to 10% after 24-72h with automatic rollback on key metric regressions, (4) full rollout. In parallel run an on-prem benchmark week where we test capacity under realistic traffic and failures.
[08:01] Priyanka: what triggers automatic rollback? absolute drop in the chosen metric or a relative change?
[08:07] Samira: we set absolute thresholds for safety metrics (e.g., hallucination incidents > 0.1% triggers rollback) and a relative drop for overall accuracy beyond agreed delta. thresholds are configurable per deployment.
[08:18] Maya: okay, makes sense. small question on FP8 — you mentioned FP8 simulated earlier. how stable is FP8 across GPUs?
[08:25] Samira: FP8 support is improving; on newer runtimes with fused kernels it's fast and accuracy can be near FP16 for many workloads. but it's hardware dependent. on A100-v5 it's good, but some older cards show more numeric instability. also FP8 quantization requires careful per-tensor scaling and occasionally dynamic overflow handling.
[08:41] Jon: for Private we'll recommend pinned GPU images and a controlled runtime; we can provide a recommended AMI/container that matches kernels used in Redwood Hosted so outputs are comparable.
[08:52] Alex: good. any more immediate questions?
[08:54] Caleb: timeline — how long to get the 1k sweep and the triage report?
[08:58] Alex: we'll aim for the 1k sweep results and short triage by 2026-04-02 and the full report + recommended hybrid profile by 2026-04-09.
[09:06] Maya: great.

--- (mid call heavy technical discussion, timestamps jump ahead; transcript has some noisy ASR artifacts) ---

[29:12] Samira: quick note — when you saw the hallucination cases, were they reproducible deterministically with seed control?
[29:19] Maya: yes reproducible about 80% of the time with same seed and prompt.
[29:23] Samira: that suggests quantization shifted the argmax in the softmax and not just RNG noise. we'll focus on per-layer reconstruction error for the affected layers.
[29:31] Alex: another tactic — layer-gating fallback: during rollout, if a critical prompt matches a watchlist pattern, run the last 4 layers on FP16 as a safety fallback. cost higher but limited to watchlist traffic.
[29:44] Caleb: can you estimate cost overhead for that?
[29:47] Alex: rough back-of-envelope: if watchlist is 1% of traffic, and last-4-layers FP16 increases compute by ~15% per-request, overall cost < 0.2% of spend but big safety value. we'll put numbers in the report.
[29:59] Priyanka: logging and audit — can you log hashed prompts or full prompts? we need to balance privacy.
[30:05] Jon: we recommend hashed prompt digests for most use, full prompts for flagged incidents with customer-side retention policies. our private control plane supports this.

[41:10] Samira: a quick summary of the technical actionables: matrix runs (batch x cache x quant method), per-layer ablation, stochastic vs deterministic rounding A/B, kernel perf by sequence length, and token-level diffs + failing traces.
[41:25] Maya: perfect. also please include a short section on how to set the SLO thresholds; we need examples.
[41:31] Alex: yes — we'll provide recommended thresholds tuned for clinical use cases.
[41:36] Caleb: and the perf harness — include example scripts for A100-v5 and a set of perf counters to capture.
[41:43] Jon: noted. we'll include nvprof/otrace commands and our preferred telemetry layout.

[50:10] Alex: ok last part — scheduling: Jon will share the VPC/KMS diagram by 2026-03-30, Samira will share the sweep scripts and seed-controlled harness, Alex will send pilot pricing and the canary rollout template. then we'll get a week booked for on-prem benchmark early April.
[50:30] Maya: thanks all, this was useful.
[50:34] Priyanka: thanks.
[50:36] Samira: thanks everyone.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
